name: Dermablend / tattoo cover

card.summary: High-coverage camouflage makeup used to hide tattoos, scars and discoloration; effects are cosmetic and temporary.
card.aka: Dermablend, Covermark, cover-up makeup, tattoo concealer
card.note: No clinical efficacy data found; coverage wears off and needs reapplication.

quick.overview:
Dermablend is a brand of high-coverage camouflage makeup, and "tattoo cover" refers to concealers of this type used to mask tattoos, scars, birthmarks and discoloration on the face or body.

Wikipedia describes cosmetic camouflage as creams or powders that hide color or texture irregularities, first developed by plastic surgeons during World War II for burns. No published trials of specific products were found.
quick.mechanism: Opaque, pigment-rich creams or powders are applied over the skin to match surrounding skin tone and hide underlying color. Color-correcting shades such as green are suggested to neutralise redness.[1]
quick.risks: Wikipedia's article does not list specific risks. As with other cosmetics, ingredients can cause irritation or allergic reactions in some people, and the makeup wears off and must be reapplied.

lead: Tattoo cover products are camouflage makeups designed to conceal tattoos, scars, vitiligo patches, bruises and other skin irregularities with heavier coverage than everyday foundation. Dermablend is one commercial brand in this category.

Wikipedia's cosmetic camouflage article says these creams were first developed by plastic surgeons during World War II to cover severe burns on pilots, and that the approach may reduce the psychological impact of skin imperfections; the article gives no clinical efficacy data and does not discuss specific brands.[1]
infobox: World War II burn camouflage creams

paras: Cosmetic camouflage refers to creams or powders used to hide color or texture irregularities on the face or body. It is also called cover makeup or corrective makeup, and is used for vitiligo, scars, tattoos, burns, acne, stretch marks, bruises, birthmarks and rosacea by men, women and children.[1]
According to Wikipedia, cosmetic camouflage creams were first developed by plastic surgeons during World War II to cover severe burns on fighter pilots.[1]

For redness, the article suggests a green concealer applied sparingly to neutralise the color.[1] Camouflage makeup is not permanent and does not change the underlying skin or tattoo. Product-specific claims by manufacturers were not reviewed here.
